title: Sarde in Saor
subtitle: Venetian sweet-and-sour marinated sardines
excerpt: Sarde in saor is one of Venice's oldest recipes -- fried fish layered with sweet slow-cooked onions, vinegar, and sometimes sultanas and pine nuts. The dish is made ahead and eaten cold, getting better as it rests. It was originally a way of preserving fish on long sea voyages.
sourceNotes: A Venetian dish dating back to the thirteenth century. It is traditionally eaten during the Feast of the Redeemer in July, but Venetians eat it year-round as a cicchetti bar snack.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make at least 4 hours ahead -- ideally overnight. Keeps refrigerated for 3 days.

content.text: This dish improves with time. Do not skip the resting step -- it is what makes saor taste like saor.

items.prepNote: use 400g fresh sardines, cleaned and filleted
use 50g sultanas and 30g pine nuts if you have them

content.text: Dust the sardine fillets lightly in flour on both sides. Shake off any excess.
Heat the vegetable oil in a frying pan over a medium-high heat. Fry the fillets for 2 minutes per side until golden. Drain on kitchen paper.
Wipe out the pan. Heat the olive oil over a low heat. Add the onions and cook very slowly for 20 minutes, stirring often, until soft and golden.
Add the vinegar, bay leaves, and sultanas and pine nuts if using. Simmer for 5 minutes. Remove from the heat.
Layer the fish and onion mixture in a bowl or dish, starting and finishing with onions.
Leave to cool, then cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours before serving cold.

items.cause: The vinegar is dominant if the onions did not cook down enough, or the resting time was too short.
items.fix: Next time cook the onions for the full 20 minutes and let the dish rest overnight. A little more honey can also balance the acidity.

items.cause: Sardines are delicate and break if handled too much during frying.
items.fix: Fry in a single layer without moving them until a crust forms. Use a wide spatula to turn once only.

items.symptom: The onions are browning rather than softening
items.cause: The heat was too high for the slow-cooking stage.
items.fix: Keep the heat on low and add a splash of water if the onions start to colour too fast.

content.text: Saor is the defining flavour of the Venetian table. You find it in every bacaro wine bar as a small cicchetti plate. The combination of sweet onion and sour vinegar appears across the whole Adriatic coastline. In Venice it is as much a summer tradition as it is a recipe.
